blocks.text: Further, because honey is not only sweet but also ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων [archē glykasmatōn], it follows that whatever is either sweet to the taste or pleasing and delightful to the mind is compared with honey. Thus it is said of the Manna in Exod. XVI, 31. And its taste was כצפיחת בדבש, like cakes with honey, that is, honeyed. For the food was so sweet that the author of Wisdom seems to regard it as a kind of ambrosia, when he calls it εὔτηκτον γένος ἀμβροσίας τροφῆς [eutēkton genos ambrosias trophēs], ch. 19, 20. By this very name honey is called by an ancient Poet,
— — — ἡ δὲ μελισσῶν Ἀμβροσίη, πυκναί τ' ἰτρίνεαι ποπάδες· [hē de melissōn Ambrosiē, pyknai t' itrineai popades]

The ambrosia of bees, and many very thin cakes. So Suidas quotes it under Ποπάδες [Popades]. And the Prophetic scroll was to Ezekiel and John sweeter than honey, Ezech. III, 3. Apoc. X, 9. 10. So too the commandments of the Lord, of which David says, Psal. XIX, 11: They are sweeter than honey and the dripping of honeycombs. And Psal. CXIX, 103: How sweet have your words been to my palate, more than honey to my mouth. Likewise divine wisdom, Prov. XXIV, 13. 14: My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the honeycomb, which is sweet to your palate. So shall the knowledge of wisdom (be sweet) to your soul, if you find it, [col. 524] etc. And Sirach. XXIV, 19. 20. (var. 26. 27.) Wisdom herself says: Come to me, you who desire me, and be filled with my fruits: for the remembrance of me is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance than the honeycomb. In Greek, Ὑπὲρ μέλιτος κηροῦ [Hyper melitos kērou]; others read κυροῦ [kyrou], others κληροῦ [klērou], others κηρίου [kēriou], others κυρίου [kyriou]. Perhaps the author had written in one word μελικήρου [melikērou], for μελίκηρος [melikēros] is a honeycomb. The word is not found in the Lexicons, but it is read in Theocritus, Idyll. 20.
— — — ἐκ στομάτων δὲ Ἔῤῥεέ μοι φωνὰ γλυκερωτέρα, ἢ μελικήρῳ· [ek stomatōn de Errhee moi phōna glykerōtera, ē melikērō]

And from my mouth flowed a voice sweeter than the honeycomb. From there the Son of Sirach could have taken it, for he wrote a few years after Theocritus, and both in Egypt. This conjecture is supported by the Syriac and Arabic versions, for both have simply honeycomb here, not honeycomb of honey. But Jerome has honey and honeycomb. In the same book, ch. 49, 2, the memory or mention of Josiah ἐν παντὶ στόματι ὡς μέλι γλυκανθήσεται [en panti stomati hōs meli glykanthēsetai], will be sweet as honey in every mouth. And of the bridegroom we read in the Chaldee paraphrast, Cantic. V, 6. מלי מוריגוי מתוקן כרבשא, The words of his palate are sweet as honey; for the Hebrew חכו ממתקים, His palate is sweetnesses. And of the bride, Cant. IV, 11: Your lips drip the honeycomb, honey and milk are under your tongue. So the poet says of Nestor, Iliad α, line 249:
[III, 386] Τοῦ καὶ ἀπὸ γλώσσης μέλιτος γλυκίον ῥεὲν αὐδής, [Tou kai apo glōssēs melitos glykion rheen audēs]
From whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey. And Theocritus, Idyll. 8:
Κρεῖσσον μελπομένῳ τεῦ ἀκουέμεν, ἢ μέλι λείχειν. [Kreisson melpomenō teu akouemen, ē meli leichein.]
It is better to hear you singing than to lick honey. And Moschus of Love, Idyll. 1:
— — — ὡς μέλι φωνὰ, [hōs meli phōna]

His voice (is sweet) as honey ^{(9)}. Which Solomon says of the harlot, Prov. V, 3: The lips of the strange woman drip the honeycomb. And Statius of Glaucias in the Epicedium, book 2 of the Silvae, [III, 387] — — — and deep within, as he spoke, his voice was mingled with Hyblaean honeycombs. — —

Hence throughout Pindar ^{n)} μελιγάρυες ὕμνοι [meligaryes hymnoi], and ^{o)} μελίφθογγοι ἀοιδαί [meliphthongoi aoidai]. And, in Illustrius, Sophocles, the tragedian, μέλιττα ἐκαλεῖτο διὰ τὸ ἡδὺ [melitta ekaleito dia to hēdy], was called a bee because of the sweetness of his verse: as Xenophon in Suidas is Ἀττικὴ μέλιττα [Attikē melitta], the Attic bee. And in Aristophanes' Birds,
— — ὥσπερ ἡ μέλιττα Φρύνιχος ἀμβροσίων Μελέων ἀπεβόσκετο καρπὸν ἀεὶ, Φέρων γλυκεῖαν ᾠδάν· [hōsper hē melitta Phrynichos ambrosiōn Meleōn apebosketo karpon aei, Pherōn glykeian ōdan]
Like a bee, Phrynichus (the comic poet) always fed on the fruit of ambrosial songs, bringing a sweet song. And in Anthology book 5, on a statue of Sappho,
Πιερικὴ δὲ μέλιττα λιγύθροος ἕζετο Σαπφὼ, [Pierikē de melitta ligythroos hezeto Sapphō]
And there sat the sweet-sounding Pierian bee, Sappho. And on Erinna,
Πιερικῆς ῥαθάμιγγας ἀποσταλάουσα μελίσσης, [Pierikēs rhathamingas apostalaousa melissēs]
Dripping the drops of the Pierian bee. And on Homer,
Πιερικὴ δὲ μέλισσα περὶ στόμα θεῖον ἀλᾶτο, Κηρίον ὠδίνουσα μελισταγές· — — [Pierikē de melissa peri stoma theion alato, Kērion ōdinousa melistages]

And the Pierian bee wandered about his divine mouth, bringing forth a honeycomb dripping with honey. To the same point belongs what Pliny ^{p)} and others ^{q)} report, that bees settled on the mouth of the infant Plato, foretelling the charm of his exceedingly sweet eloquence. Authors not to be despised write the same of Pindar ^{r)}, Lucan ^{s)} and Ambrose ^{t)}.
